Well, I want this search engine to have a basic fast mode, which is the gpt oss 120b-OSS 120B model, because it's the fastest in the world and is integrated with the Exa AI search engine. Every search should always be set to a fixed one hundred hits, because that's how I want it, and that's that.
It should be in fast mode because that's the point of fast mode: the world's fastest search API is the Exa AI fast mode, and its fastest inference model. Then there will be the other one, Pro mode, where an agent is composed of multiple models, like Grok 4 Heavy, which is built from multiple models. It's so big that it can search completely autonomously for hours—even up to five hours—while improving itself, and at the end, it writes a 500-kilobyte text file, which is the report. I want it to be like AI Deep Research: I type in what I want, attach a file or key, and then it creates a plan, sends it to me, I approve it, and then it researches. Or I edit it, approve it again, and then it researches again.
I planned to integrate multiple models from Grok 4, as well as the Claude Opus 4.5 model from Amazon Bedrock and Gemini with a GCP key, i.e., Gemini 3 Pro. Among the search engines, I want to integrate Exa AI, as well as Parallel, specifically the Ultra Deep Research mode, and X8, because it can search from 16,000 sources.
Meanwhile, after about 10 minutes, it creates a sub-report, which is also long and is actually a full-fledged research report. In the meantime, it is possible for the model, the agent, to continue searching, but at the same time, everything can be attached to it. In the chat, the model itself should recognize the platform, see that research is in progress, and be able to answer how long it will take, and so on.
1. Architecture Structure
The system is a hierarchy-free network: an orchestrator coordinates, but there is no boss-subordinate relationship. Main components:
• Input Processor: Evaluates the complexity of the query (Grok 4 single call, prompt: "Rate the complexity of [query] on a scale of 1-10: 1=simple factual question, 10=PhD-level problem"). If <=5, single-agent mode (direct Grok 4 call). If >5, Heavy mode: spawn N agents (N = min(32, max(5, round(complexity * 2)))). Input: query (text/image/audio multimodal). Output: N, list of roles (random/query-specific: e.g., 40% reasoner, 30% researcher, 20% critic, 10% creator).
• Agents: 5-32 independent Grok 4 instances with specialized prompts. Each agent receives: query copy + role prompt + tools. Processing: chain-of-thought hypothesis generation (1-3), tool call if necessary (e.g., code_execution for math), self-reflection (confidence 0-1). Output: JSON structure.
• Orchestrator: Collects agent outputs, runs the debate phase (with Grok 4 call), builds consensus. Maximum 3 iterations in case of conflict. Tools: orchestrator can also call if necessary (e.g., web_search for validation).
• Output Synthesizer: Summarizes consensus with Grok 4 (prompt: explanation + alternatives + reliability score). Output: user-friendly response (text + optional code/image).
• Tool Layer: Native Grok 4 function calling. Required tools: web_search (for facts), code_execution (with Python REPL numpy/sympy/pandas), image_analysis (from URL). Optional: x_search (for X posts). Available to all agents/orchestrators as JSON: {"name": "tool_name", "arguments": {...}}.
Data flow: Query → Input Processor → Parallel Agents → Orchestrator (debate/consensus) → Synthesizer → Response. Latency target: <5 minutes for complex queries (due to parallelism).
2. Operational Logic (Workflow)
Iterative cycle: Initialization → Parallel Execution → Debate → Consensus → Synthesis. Each step is asynchronous, with error handling (retry 3x timeout).
 * Initialization (Input Processor):
   • Call: AsyncOpenAI chat.completions.create(model="grok-4-latest", messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "Evaluator role..."}, {"role": "user", "content": query}], temperature=0.1).
   • Decision: N agents, role assignment (list: ['reasoner', 'researcher', 'critic', 'creator', 'validator'] – repeat/extend to N).
   • Prompt template for agent: “You are Agent #{id}: {role} (e.g., reasoner: step-by-step logic, focus on first principles). Task: [query]. Generate 1-3 hypotheses/calls with tools if necessary (e.g., code_execution for simulation). Output strictly JSON: {‘hypotheses’: [{‘text’: ‘…’, ‘confidence’: 0-1, ‘tools_used’: [‘tool1’]}], ‘self_eval’: ‘Strengths/weaknesses’}. Think step by step, prioritize accuracy, but keep Grok style: witty, truth-seeking.”
 * Parallel Execution (Agents):
   • Asynchronous calls: tasks = [client.chat.completions.create(…, messages=[system_prompt(role, id, query), …], tools=tool_defs, temperature=0.7) for id, role in enumerate(roles)].
   • Waiting: results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True).
   • Parse: Extract JSON from each result (validated with Pydantic model). If there is an error, use the default hypothesis (e.g., “Failed to process”).
 * Debate & Consensus (Orchestrator):
   • Collection: agents_json = [result.choices[0].message.content for result in results].
   • Call: orchestrator_call = client.chat.completions.create(messages=[{“role”: “system”, “content”: “Orchestrator prompt: Input: [agents_json]. Debate: Rate each hypothesis on a scale of 0-1 (‘Agent1 vs Agent2: refutation’). Conflict if variance >0.3: iterate with a new round (send back critiques to agents max 3x). Consensus: weighted vote (high confidence wins), tied majority. Output JSON: {‘best_hypothesis’: ‘…’, ‘alternatives’: […], ‘reliability’: avg_confidence (0-1)}.”}, {“role”: “user”, “content”: “Run the debate.”}], temperature=0.5).
   • Iteration: If there is a conflict (reliability <0.7), new parallel call agents with critiques as extra context, max 3x.
 * Synthesis (Output Synthesizer):
   • Call: final_call = client.chat.completions.create(messages=[{“role”: “system”, “content”: "Synthesizer: Based on [consensus_json], generate a user-friendly response: detailed explanation with steps, alternatives, tool resource citations, reliability score in % (if <70%, 'I recommend human review'). Maintain Grok style: helpful, witty, unfiltered truth."}, {“role”: “user”, “content”: query}], temperature=0.3).
   • Output: Response text + metadata (usage tokens, reliability).
   Error handling: All calls timeout=3600s (for reasoning models), retry with exponential backoff. Logging: JSON log for each step (to file or console).
3. Implementation Details
• SDK & Config: Use AsyncOpenAI (pip install openai). Config file (config.py): API_KEY = os.getenv(“XAI_API_KEY”), BASE_URL=“ MODEL=“grok-4-latest”.
• Tool Defs: Define as JSON schema (Grok 4 compatible): tools = [ {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "web_search", "description": "Search on the web", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"]}}}, {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "code_execution", "description": "Code execution in Python", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"code": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["code"]}}} ]
• In agent calls: tools=tools, tool_choice="auto".
• Code Structure:
• input_processor.py: async def evaluate_complexity(query): … return N, roles.
• agent.py: async def run_agent(client, id, role, query, tools): … return json.loads(content).
• orchestrator.py: async def debate_consensus(client, agents_outputs, tools): … (loop max 3x).
• synthesizer.py: async def synthesize(client, consensus, query): …
• main.py: async def heavy_query(query): processor → agents = await asyncio.gather(…) → consensus = await debate(…) → response = await synthesize(…) ; return response.content + f”\nReliability: {consensus[‘reliability’]*100:.1f}%”.
• Execution: if name == “main”: asyncio.run(heavy_query(“Example query: Solve this quantum problem.”)).
• Multimodal Support: If query image: messages-in “content”: [{“type”: “image_url”, “image_url”: {“url”: url, “detail”: “high”}}, {“type”: “text”, “text”: query_text}].
TiffyTime Pro Structure Plan
(Built into main.py)
The goal: to create multiple independent thought paths and then coordinate them for a more reliable answer.
2. Orchestrator Layer Logic
 * Task reception and analysis:
   The first step is to interpret the incoming question—how complex it is, what type it is (factual, creative, analytical, computational). This determines how many independent agents should be launched. Simple questions require fewer agents, while complex problems require more.
 * Dynamic resource allocation:
   The orchestrator decides how much computational capacity to allocate to the task. Each agent needs a separate process or thread to operate completely independently of the others.
3. Query Decomposition - Perspective Generation
 * Developing a multi-faceted approach:
   You don't simply copy the original question to every agent, but generate different perspectives. For example, for a complex question:
   * One agent approaches it from a critical, skeptical point of view.
   * Another agent is optimistic and solution-oriented.
   * A third agent is purely analytical and data-driven.
   * A fourth agent is creative and unconventional.
 * System prompt design:
   You generate a unique system message for each agent, which shapes their thinking style, but they all receive the same question. The variability is in the approach, not in the question.
4. Parallel Execution Architecture
 * Principle of independent execution:
   All agents start working at the same moment in time, but completely isolated from each other. They cannot see each other's intermediate results or thought processes. This ensures that each agent truly reaches an independent conclusion.
 * Process monitoring:
   The orchestrator tracks where each agent is, but does not interfere with their work. If an agent runs too long or stops, it must be detected, but the others continue their work.
5. Response Collection and Structuring
 * Uniform output format:
   When an agent finishes, the result must be organized into a structured format. The final answer alone is not enough—the following is also needed:
   * The text of the answer.
   * The steps in the reasoning chain.
   * The sources, if external information was used.
   * The agent's own level of certainty in the answer.
 * Timeout handling:
   If an agent does not finish on time, the orchestrator does not wait for it indefinitely. Beyond a predefined time limit, the system continues with the results of the other agents.
6. Cross-Validation Mechanism
 * Semantic comparison:
   You don't compare the responses of different agents literally, but at the level of meaning. To do this, you convert the responses into embedding vectors and calculate how similar they are to each other conceptually.
 * Cluster formation:
   Similar responses are organized into natural groups. For example, if five out of three agents came to the same conclusion (in different words), that is one cluster. If two went in completely different directions, those are separate clusters.
 * Outlier identification:
   Answers that stand alone and do not fit anywhere must be marked. These may be incorrect or possibly creative, non-obvious solutions.
7. Consensus Algorithm
 * Weighted voting system:
   This is not a simple majority vote, but rather each agent's response is weighted along several dimensions:
   * How many other agents reached a similar conclusion (cluster size).
   * How confident was the agent according to its own assessment.
   * How coherent is the chain of reasoning.
   * If an external source was used, how reliable is it.
 * Convergence assessment:
   You examine the degree of agreement. If a large majority agrees, there is clear consensus. If opinions are divided, there is low consensus.
 * Threshold-based decision:
   If a certain percentage of agents agree, that becomes the basis for the final answer. If this level is not reached, the goal is not a single answer, but a synthesis of multiple perspectives.
8. Synthesis Layer - Meta-Reasoning
 * Handling low consensus:
   If there is no clear winning cluster, you call a meta-agent. This is another LLM call, but now the input is the responses and reasoning of all previous agents.
 * Synthesis logic:
   The meta-agent does not vote, but integrates. It understands why the agents said different things and constructs a higher-level response that takes all perspectives into account.
 * Uncertainty signaling:
   If the meta-agent cannot give a clear answer either, it must be made transparent—the final output includes that the question can be interpreted in multiple ways.
9. Final Response Assembly
 * Hierarchical response structure:
   The final output is layered:
   * At the top is the direct response (provided by consensus or synthesis).
   * Below that is a detailed explanation.
   * If there were alternative points of view, they are also included.
   * Transparency layer: how many agents thought what.
 * Attaching metadata:
   In addition to the response, you provide information about how reliable the result is—how much consensus there was, how many agents worked on it, how long it took.
10. Feedback Loop and Iteration
 * Self-reflection mechanism:
   Optionally, a validation phase may follow, where a separate agent reviews the final answer and validates it with external sources or logical consistency checks.
 * Uncertainty triggered re-run:
   If the system detects that the certainty is too low, it can automatically re-run the process with more agents or different parameters.
11. Orchestration Flow Control
 * Handoff pattern:
   If an agent realizes during the process that a subtask requires specialized knowledge (e.g., complex mathematics), it can hand it over to a specialized sub-agent and then retrieve the result.
 * Dynamic replanning:
   If, during execution, it turns out that the question means something different than what was initially interpreted, the orchestrator can replan the strategy—it can stop agents and start new ones.
12. Complete Process Summary
Input Query 
↓
Orchestrator analyzes 
↓
Perspective generation 
↓
N independent agents start in parallel
↓
Each thinks independently, using tools
↓
Responses collection in a uniform format
↓
Semantic comparison → clustering
↓
Weighted consensus calculation
↓
├─ If high consensus → winning cluster response
└─ If low consensus → meta-agent synthesis
↓
Final response assembly + metadata
↓
Optional: validation loop
↓
Output to User

• Problem resolution: When it receives a complex user query, the system first compiles a detailed research plan by breaking the problem down into smaller, more manageable subtasks. The plan is under your control: TiffyTime shows you the plan, and you can refine it to ensure that it focuses on the right areas.
• Research: TiffyTime oversees the execution of the plan and intelligently determines which subtasks can be managed simultaneously and which must be performed sequentially. Among other things, TiffyTime can collect and think through information using search and web browsing. At each step, it considers the available information to decide what to do next. We have introduced a thought process panel where users can track what TiffyTime has found so far and what it intends to do next.
• Summary: When TiffyTime decides that it has gathered enough information, it summarizes its findings in a comprehensive report. When compiling the report, TiffyTime critically evaluates the information, identifies important topics and inconsistencies, structures the report in a logical and informative way, and takes even more self-critical steps to ensure that the results are as clear and detailed as possible.
Multi-step planning
Research tasks require multi-step iterative planning. At each step, TiffyTime must validate the information collected so far and then figure out what missing information and inconsistencies to focus on—while balancing the time required for detailed research with the time required for computation and user waiting time. Because we trained TiffyTime to be able to plan longer, multi-step tasks in a data-efficient way, we were able to make Deep Research work on any topic (this is called an "open domain" system).
During a typical Deep Research task, numerous TiffyTime calls are made over several minutes. This poses a challenge when creating agents, because they must be designed so that a single error does not require the entire task to be restarted.
To address this challenge, we developed a novel asynchronous task manager that maintains a shared state between the planning and task TiffyTime, allowing for more forgiving recovery from errors without restarting the entire task. This system actually works asynchronously: after starting a Deep Research project, you can switch to another application or even turn off your computer, and the next time you visit TiffyTime, you will receive a notification that your research is complete.
Context management
During a given research session, TiffyTime can process up to several hundred pages of content. To maintain continuity and enable follow-up questions, TiffyTime uses a one-million-token context window, unique in the industry, supplemented by the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) method. This essentially allows the system to "remember" everything it has learned during a given chat session, so the longer you interact with it, the smarter it becomes.

   You examine the degree of agreement. If a large majority agrees, there is clear consensus. If opinions are divided, there is low consensus.
 * Threshold-based decision:
   If a certain percentage of agents agree, that becomes the basis for the final answer. If this level is not reached, the goal is not a single answer, but a synthesis of multiple perspectives.
8. Synthesis Layer - Meta-Reasoning
 * Handling low consensus:
   If there is no clear winning cluster, you call a meta-agent. This is another LLM call, but now the input is the responses and reasoning of all previous agents.
 * Synthesis logic:
   The meta-agent does not vote, but integrates. It understands why the agents said different things and constructs a higher-level response that takes all perspectives into account.
 * Uncertainty signaling:
   If the meta-agent cannot give a clear answer either, it must be made transparent—the final output includes that the question can be interpreted in multiple ways.
9. Final Response Assembly
 * Hierarchical response structure:
   The final output is layered:
   * At the top is the direct response (provided by consensus or synthesis).
   * Below that is a detailed explanation.
   * If there were alternative points of view, they are also included.
   * Transparency layer: how many agents thought what.
 * Attaching metadata:
   In addition to the response, you provide information about how reliable the result is—how much consensus there was, how many agents worked on it, how long it took.
10. Feedback Loop and Iteration
 * Self-reflection mechanism:
   Optionally, a validation phase may follow, where a separate agent reviews the final answer and validates it with external sources or logical consistency checks.
 * Uncertainty triggered re-run:
   If the system detects that the certainty is too low, it can automatically re-run the process with more agents or different parameters.
11. Orchestration Flow Control
 * Handoff pattern:
   If an agent realizes during the process that a subtask requires specialized knowledge (e.g., complex mathematics), it can hand it over to a specialized sub-agent and then retrieve the result.
 * Dynamic replanning:
   If, during execution, it turns out that the question means something different than what was initially interpreted, the orchestrator can replan the strategy—it can stop agents and start new ones.
12. Complete Process Summary
Input Query 
↓
Orchestrator analyzes 
↓
Perspective generation 
↓
N independent agents start in parallel
↓
Each thinks independently, using tools
↓
Responses collection in a uniform format
↓
Semantic comparison → clustering
↓
Weighted consensus calculation
↓
├─ If high consensus → winning cluster response
└─ If low consensus → meta-agent synthesis
↓
Final response assembly + metadata
↓
Optional: validation loop
↓
Output to User

• Problem resolution: When it receives a complex user query, the system first compiles a detailed research plan by breaking the problem down into smaller, more manageable subtasks. The plan is under your control: TiffyTime shows you the plan, and you can refine it to ensure that it focuses on the right areas.
• Research: TiffyTime oversees the execution of the plan and intelligently determines which subtasks can be managed simultaneously and which must be performed sequentially. Among other things, TiffyTime can collect and think through information using search and web browsing. At each step, it considers the available information to decide what to do next. We have introduced a thought process panel where users can track what TiffyTime has found so far and what it intends to do next.
• Summary: When TiffyTime decides that it has gathered enough information, it summarizes its findings in a comprehensive report. When compiling the report, TiffyTime critically evaluates the information, identifies important topics and inconsistencies, structures the report in a logical and informative way, and takes even more self-critical steps to ensure that the results are as clear and detailed as possible.
Multi-step planning
Research tasks require multi-step iterative planning. At each step, TiffyTime must validate the information collected so far and then figure out what missing information and inconsistencies to focus on—while balancing the time required for detailed research with the time required for computation and user waiting time. Because we trained TiffyTime to be able to plan longer, multi-step tasks in a data-efficient way, we were able to make Deep Research work on any topic (this is called an "open domain" system).
During a typical Deep Research task, numerous TiffyTime calls are made over several minutes. This poses a challenge when creating agents, because they must be designed so that a single error does not require the entire task to be restarted.
To address this challenge, we developed a novel asynchronous task manager that maintains a shared state between the planning and task TiffyTime, allowing for more forgiving recovery from errors without restarting the entire task. This system actually works asynchronously: after starting a Deep Research project, you can switch to another application or even turn off your computer, and the next time you visit TiffyTime, you will receive a notification that your research is complete.
Context management
During a given research session, TiffyTime can process up to several hundred pages of content. To maintain continuity and enable follow-up questions, TiffyTime uses a one-million-token context window, unique in the industry, supplemented by the RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) method. This essentially allows the system to "remember" everything it has learned during a given chat session, so the longer you interact with it, the smarter it becomes.

A csatolt `file-1.py` teljes tartalma nem áll rendelkezésre teljes terjedelemben, csak egy részlete látható, ezért nem lehet biztonságosan „minden egyes karaktert” tartalmazó, 100%-ban konzisztens és hibamentes, frissített teljes fájlt visszaadni.[1]
A jelenleg elérhető részlet alapján a fájl egy Flask alkalmazás Cerebras klienssel, in-memory store-okkal és auth endpointokkal indul, de a további részek hiánya miatt nem garantálható a teljes kód helyes egyben tartása és a kért architektúra hibamentes beépítése.[1]

## Mi hiányzik a teljes visszaadáshoz
A kért „teljes kódot visszaküldöd, nem rövidítesz” feltételhez szükséges a teljes forrás (a fájl vége, minden route, helper, import, futtatási blokk), mert különben nem lehet ellenőrizni az összes névütközést, függőséget, útvonalat, és a futásidejű hibákat.[1]
Most csak a fájl elejéről látható egy rész (Flask init, session/auth váz, Cerebras kliens létrehozás, index route, stb.), ami nem elég a teljes, production-ready újratervezéshez és egyben visszaadásához.[1]

## Mit küldj, hogy megkapd a teljes kódot
Illeszd be ide a `file-1.py` teljes tartalmát egyben (a legelső sortól az utolsóig), vagy töltsd fel úgy, hogy a teljes szöveg kiolvasható legyen, mert csak így tud a frissített verzió 1 fájlban, rövidítés nélkül elkészülni.[1]
Emellett pontosítsd, hogy a végső app maradjon-e Flask (és milyen futtatási környezetben: gunicorn/uvicorn, Modal.com entrypoint), illetve a kulcsok neveit véglegesítsük-e az általad megadott környezetváltozó-nevekkel (xAI/AWS/GCP/Exa/Parallel/Dragonfly/Supermemory).[1]

Melyik formában kéred a teljes fájlt: ide bemásolod a teljes `file-1.py`-t, vagy feltöltesz egy új csatolmányt, ami biztosan teljes terjedelemben olvasható?
